(CNN) -- After a nearly decade-long effort, the National Congress of Black Women on Tuesday honored Sojourner Truth by making her the first African-American woman to have a memorial bust in the U.S. Capitol. Speaker Nancy Pelosi and first lady Michelle Obama applaud the unveiling of the Sojourner Truth bust. Truth, whose given name was Isabella Baumfree, was a slave who became one of the most respected abolitionists and women's rights activists. "One could only imagine what Sojourner Truth, an outspoken, tell-it-like-it-is kind of woman ... what she would have to say about this incredible gathering," first lady Michelle Obama said at the Celebration of Truth ceremony. "We are all here because, as my husband says time and time again, we stand on the shoulders of giants like Sojourner Truth." "And just as Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott would be pleased to know that we have a woman serving as the speaker of the House of Representatives, I hope that Sojourner Truth would be proud to see me, a descendant of slaves, serving as the first lady of the United States of America," she said. Dignitaries and congressional leaders, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, House Republican Leader John Boehner and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, attended the ceremony marking the unveiling of the statue. Along with musical performances, actress Cicely Tyson recited "Ain't I A Woman," Truth's famous 1851 speech to a women's rights convention. Clinton and Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee, who worked together to draft legislation to commission the bust, were among speakers who paid tribute to the late C. Delores Tucker, former chairwoman of the NCBW, who spearheaded the effort for the Truth memorial. "What a wonderful day it is to be here in Emancipation Hall for this great occasion when Sojourner Truth takes her rightful place alongside the heroes who have helped to shape our nation's history," Clinton said. "Today, she takes her place in this Capitol, and we are the better for it," Clinton said. "She is a sojourner of truth, by truth, and for truth. And her words, her example and her legacy will never perish from this earth, so long as men and women stand up and say loudly and clearly, 'We hear you echoing down through the years of history. We believe that your journey is not yet over, and we will make the rest of that journey with you.' " The bronze statue, which was crafted by Los Angeles, California, sculptor Artis Lane, will stand in Emancipation Hall at the Capitol Visitor Center. "All the visitors in the U.S. Capitol will hear the story of brave women who endured the greatest of humanity's indignities. They'll hear the story of Sojourner Truth, who didn't allow those indignities to destroy her spirit, who fought for her own freedom and then used her powers ... to help others," Michelle Obama said. "The power of this bust will not just be in the metal that delineates Sojourner Truth's face; it will also be in the message that defines her legacy. Forevermore, in the halls of one of our country's greatest monuments of liberty and equality, justice and freedom, Sojourner Truth's story will be told again and again and again and again." In 1997, Congress passed a special act that called for relocating the Portrait Monument from the Capitol basement to the rotunda. The 7.5-ton statue depicts three leaders of the suffragette movement -- Anthony, Stanton and Mott. A group called the Sojourner Truth Crusade was upset about the statue's relocation because it didn't incorporate Truth. After Congress agreed to go ahead with a move, advocates proposed commissioning a new statue that would include Truth. In 2006, Congress passed a bill to honor the abolitionist with her own memorial.

**A Monumental Step: How Sojourner Truth Became the First Black Woman Memorialized in the U.S. Capitol**

In April 2009, beneath the vaulted ceilings of Emancipation Hall in the United States Capitol Visitor Center, history was both honored and made. Before a crowd of lawmakers, civil rights icons, and citizens, a bronze bust of abolitionist and women’s rights pioneer Sojourner Truth was officially unveiled. The moment marked a watershed achievement: Truth became the first African-American woman to be permanently memorialized in the seat of American democracy. This historic occasion was not merely the unveiling of a statue, but the culmination of a ten-year legislative crusade—a testament to how far the nation had traveled from the horrors of slavery to the heights of modern political leadership.

### A Decade-Long Crusade for Recognition

The path to placing Sojourner Truth in the Capitol was long and fraught with legislative hurdles. For decades, the Capitol’s extensive collection of statues and busts overwhelmingly represented white male historical figures, reflecting the skewed demographics of those who held power throughout early American history. 

Recognizing this glaring absence, the National Congress of Black Women (NCBW)—initially led by the late Dr. C. DeLores Tucker and later carried forward by Dr. E. Faye Williams—launched a campaign in the late 1990s to secure a permanent place for Truth in the Capitol. The initiative gained vital momentum when key congressional leaders stepped forward to champion the cause. Representative Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas introduced the necessary legislation in the House, while then-Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton pushed the bill through the Senate.

The effort faced bureaucratic obstacles, as federal law strictly regulated the addition of new sculptures to the Capitol’s National Statuary Hall Collection, which traditionally required states to submit statues of their own choosing. However, through persistent advocacy, Congress passed legislation in 2006 authorizing the acceptance of the bust, directing it to be placed in the newly constructed Capitol Visitor Center.

### The Voice of Freedom and Equality

The woman honored by this monumental effort was born into slavery as Isabella Baumfree in Ulster County, New York, around 1797. After escaping to freedom with her infant daughter in 1826, she adopted the name Sojourner Truth in 1843, declaring that God had called her to travel the country and proclaim the truth of human equality.

Truth became one of the most powerful orators of the 19th century. Standing over six feet tall, with a commanding voice and unwavering conviction, she bridged the gap between the abolitionist movement and the early women’s suffrage movement. Her iconic, improvised speech at the 1851 Women’s Rights Convention in Akron, Ohio—famously remembered for the repeated phrase, *"Ain't I a Woman?"*—challenged both the racism of white suffragists and the sexism of male abolitionists. Truth demanded an intersectional vision of freedom that recognized the dignity, humanity, and rights of Black women long before the term "intersectionality" existed.

### A Historic Ceremony and Artistic Triumph

The 2009 unveiling ceremony was a deeply symbolic gathering of American leadership. Among those presiding over the event were House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and First Lady Michelle Obama—the nation’s first African-American First Lady. 

In a moving address, Michelle Obama reflected on the profound historical arc represented by the monument. She noted that it was fitting for Truth to be honored in a hall built in part by the labor of enslaved people, standing alongside the very lawmakers who carry on the work of American governance. “I hope that Sojourner Truth would be proud to see me, a descendant of slaves, serving as First Lady of the United States,” Obama remarked, underscoring the deep connection between Truth’s 19th-century struggle and 21st-century progress.

The bronze bust itself was crafted by renowned sculptor Artis Lane, making Lane the first Black woman to be commissioned to create a statue for the U.S. Capitol. Lane depicted Truth not as a somber victim of oppression, but with a warm, knowing smile, draped in her characteristic cap and shawl—capturing both her formidable intellect and her deep humanity.

### An Enduring Legacy

The permanent inclusion of Sojourner Truth in the U.S. Capitol is far more than a decorative addition; it is an act of historical justice. For millions of visitors who walk through Emancipation Hall each year, her presence serves as a powerful reminder that the story of American democracy was written not only by its Founding Fathers, but also by the marginalized men and women who fought tirelessly to force the nation to live up to its founding ideals.

By cementing Truth’s place among the nation’s key historical figures, the United States Capitol embraced a fuller, more truthful rendering of its past. Sojourner Truth’s bronze gaze now permanently rests upon the halls of power, offering an enduring symbol of resilience, progress, and the unbreakable spirit of those who demand justice.

**Echoes Behind the Screen: Journalism and the National Discourse**

The hum of a major television newsroom is a unique kind of electricity. For hours on end, anchors, producers, and field reporters work in a synchronized frenzy, translating complex, rapidly evolving events into a coherent narrative for millions of viewers across the country. As a pioneer of the 24-hour news cycle, **CNN** has long occupied a central seat at this table, shaping how the public consumes breaking news during moments of profound importance.

Yet, the true weight of broadcast journalism is often felt most acutely **after** the cameras stop rolling. 

When covering a major **national** event—whether it is a pivotal presidential election, a historic legislative vote, or a coast-to-coast crisis—the immediate pressure on a news organization is speed and accuracy. In the heat of the moment, the goal is simply to keep the public informed as history unfolds in real time. However, once the live segment ends and the red "On Air" light turns off, a different phase of journalism begins: the work of contextualization and reflection.

In the hours and days following a massive broadcast, media outlets must look beyond the immediate adrenaline of the headline. It is during this crucial period that the true contours of a **national** story take shape. Analysts and reporters digest the data, vet new sources, and begin answering the deeper questions: What do these events mean for everyday citizens? How will this shift the socio-political landscape moving forward? 

For networks like **CNN**, the responsibility extends far beyond being first to break a story. It lies in maintaining editorial integrity long **after** the initial wave of breaking news subsides. In a fast-paced media ecosystem, the lasting legacy of any news organization is defined not just by how it covers the crisis of the moment, but by how it helps a nation understand the path ahead once the noise begins to clear.

**WASHINGTON — April 28, 2009** — In a ceremony rich with song, tears, and bipartisan reverence, top political figures gathered Tuesday in the U.S. Capitol Visitor Center’s Emancipation Hall to unveil a bronze bust of abolitionist and suffragist Sojourner Truth. The unveiling marks the first time an African American woman has been permanently memorialized with a statue or bust within the halls of the United States Capitol.

The ceremony brought together an array of the nation's most prominent leaders, including First Lady Michelle Obama, Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton, Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, House Minority Leader John Boehner, Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, and Representative Sheila Jackson Lee (D-Texas). 

The bronze likeness—sculpted by 81-year-old artist Artis Lane—depicts Truth wearing her signature cap and shawl, rendered with a subtle, knowing smile. It stands as a powerful testament to a woman born into slavery in 1797 as Isabella Baumfree, who transformed herself into one of the 19th century’s most formidable champions for human rights.

### "A Descendant of Slaves"

First Lady Michelle Obama delivered emotional remarks, reflecting on the historical arc that brought a bust of a former slave into the Capitol during the presidency of her husband, Barack Obama, the nation's first African American president.

"I hope that Sojourner Truth would be proud of the world we live in today, calling on us to continue her work," the First Lady told a packed audience of lawmakers, civil rights leaders, and guests. 

Connecting her own presence in the White House to Truth’s legacy, Obama added: "I hope that she would be proud to see me, a descendant of slaves, serving as First Lady of the United States of America. But I know that she would not be satisfied with where we are today. She would remind us that there is still so much work to be done."

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who helped lead the legislative effort to honor Truth during her time as a U.S. senator representing New York, reflected on Truth’s famous 1851 "Ain't I a Woman?" speech delivered at the Women's Rights Convention in Akron, Ohio.

"Sojourner Truth was a woman who never let her circumstances define her, and she never let the prejudices of her era silence her," Clinton said. "Today, Sojourner Truth takes her rightful place among our nation’s founders and leaders in the place where the story of our democracy is told."

### The 2006 Legislative Victory

Tuesday's dedication was the culmination of a multi-year legislative campaign. In 2006, Representative Sheila Jackson Lee introduced H.R. 4510 in the House, while then-Senator Clinton championed companion legislation in the Senate. The bill authorized the placement of the bust in the Capitol, marking a historic shift in the Capitol's public art collection, which had long been criticized for its lack of diversity.

The legislation was passed unanimously by Congress and signed into law by President George W. Bush in December 2006. Funding for the sculpture was raised privately by the National Congress of Black Women (NCBW), spearheaded by its late founder, Dr. C. DeLores Tucker, and continued by the organization’s leadership following Tucker’s death in 2005.

### Rectifying History: The Portrait Monument Controversy

The drive to install the bust grew directly out of a decade-old controversy surrounding another Capitol artwork: the *Portrait Monument*. 

Sculpted by Adelaide Johnson in 1920, the 14-ton marble monument depicts three pioneering white suffragists: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, and Lucretia Mott. Unveiled in the Capitol Rotunda in 1921, the statue was almost immediately moved to the Capitol Crypt, where it sat in obscurity for 76 years before activists successfully lobbied to move it back to the Rotunda in 1997.

However, the *Portrait Monument* carried a painful oversight. Behind the carved busts of Stanton, Anthony, and Mott sat a large, uncarved block of marble. A popular myth persisted for decades that the unfinished marble was reserved for a Black suffragist—most often assumed to be Sojourner Truth. 

In reality, sculptor Adelaide Johnson had left the marble unfinished to symbolize that the fight for women’s equality was ongoing. Black women’s groups pointed out that the exclusion of Black suffragists from the original sculpture mirrored the historic marginalization Black women faced during the 19th-century suffrage movement, where white leaders often sidelined Black women to appease Southern political interests.

During the late 1990s and early 2000s, civil rights activists, led by the National Congress of Black Women, campaigned to have Sojourner Truth’s image sculpted into the unfinished portion of the *Portrait Monument*. When art historians, architects of the Capitol, and preservationists concluded that altering the existing marble monument was both artistically inappropriate and structurally risky, activists pivoted to push for a separate, standalone bust of Truth.

### A Permanent Place in Emancipation Hall

The resolution of that fight was visible on Tuesday in Emancipation Hall—a space inside the Capitol Visitor Center named explicitly to honor the enslaved laborers who built much of the U.S. Capitol building.

Congressional leaders from both sides of the aisle emphasized the importance of truth-telling in the Capitol's commemorative works. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi noted that Truth’s presence transforms the Capitol into a more accurate reflection of American history, while Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid praised her relentless pursuit of justice.

For those in attendance, the unveiling was a long-overdue correction of the historic record. As the cloak was pulled away to reveal the bronze face of Sojourner Truth, the crowd erupted in a standing ovation, celebrating a woman who spent her life fighting for freedom, and who now permanently stands in the center of American democracy.

**THE WASHINGTON HERALD**

**A Bronze Legend Takes Her Place: Sojourner Truth Becomes First Black Woman Honored with U.S. Capitol Bust**

**Byline:** Press Corps Reporting  
**WASHINGTON — April 28, 2009** — History echoed through the high-vaulted arches of Emancipation Hall today as Sojourner Truth, the towering 19th-century abolitionist and women's rights pioneer, permanently claimed her seat in the halls of American democracy. In a poignant, emotional ceremony, Truth became the first African-American woman to be honored with a memorial bust inside the United States Capitol.

The unveiling marks a momentous shift in the nation’s sanctuary of statues, long dominated by white, male historical figures. Flanked by nation’s top leaders—including First Lady Michelle Obama, Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi, and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton—the bronze likeness of Truth was revealed to a thunderous standing ovation from a crowd of hundreds.

"I hope that Sojourner Truth would be proud to see us all sitting here today in the shadow of her bust," said First Lady Michelle Obama, addressing the crowd. "And I hope that she would be pleased to see so many women serving in high places in our government."

### A Decades-Long Struggle: C. Delores Tucker’s Vision Realized

The road to Emancipation Hall was long and fraught with legislative hurdles. Today’s triumph was widely recognized as the posthumous victory of the late C. Delores Tucker, a fierce civil rights activist and former president of the National Congress of Black Women (NCBW). 

It was Dr. Tucker who, in the late 1990s, realized that while the Capitol held monuments to the suffragist movement—such as the massive portrait monument of Lucretia Mott, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Susan B. Anthony—it completely omitted the contributions of Black women. Tucker launched a relentless crusade to amend the omission, lobbying Congress and raising private funds to ensure Truth took her rightful place beside her contemporaries. 

Though Dr. Tucker passed away in 2005, her legacy was palpable today as members of the NCBW, wearing their signature purple, sat in the audience weeping tears of joy as her dream was finally realized.

### A Masterpiece of Resilience by Artis Lane

The monumental task of bringing Truth’s likeness to life was entrusted to renowned 81-year-old sculptor Artis Lane. Lane, the first Black woman to design an official portrait for a U.S. president, crafted a bronze bust that captures both the formidable strength and deep warmth of the iconic freedom fighter.

Lane’s sculpture depicts Truth with a gentle, knowing smile—a departure from the severe, stoic expressions common in 19th-century portraiture. Wearing a traditional bonnet and a intricately rendered quilted shawl, the bust stands atop a pedestal made of Swedish granite. 

"I wanted to depict her as a person of great dignity, intellect, and spiritual strength," Lane remarked prior to the ceremony. "She was not just a victim of her time; she was a conqueror."

### "Ain't I a Woman?": Cicely Tyson Stuns the Hall

If the veil lifting was the heart of the ceremony, its soul was delivered by legendary actress Cicely Tyson. 

Taking the podium, Tyson transformed before the eyes of the audience, channeling Truth’s fiery spirit in a spellbinding recitation of her famous 1851 Akron, Ohio speech, "Ain't I a Woman?"

With booming cadence and sharp, commanding gestures, Tyson’s voice rang through the Capitol: 

> *"That man over there says that women need to be helped into carriages, and lifted over ditches, and to have the best place everywhere. Nobody ever helps me into carriages, or over mud-puddles, or gives me any best place! And ain't I a woman?"*

The performance brought the audience to its feet, tears streaming down the faces of lawmakers and activists alike. The centuries-old words, spoken in the modern center of power, served as a stark reminder of the long, painful journey from human bondage to the highest corridors of American leadership.

### A Permanent Legacy

Born into slavery as Isabella Baumfree in 1797, Truth escaped to freedom in 1826 and spent the remainder of her life preaching the gospel of abolition and equal rights. Today, her bronze gaze rests permanently in the Capitol, ensuring that future generations of Americans will look up at her and remember the woman who dared to demand: *“Ain’t I a woman?”*

As the ceremony concluded, guests lingered around the stage, reluctant to leave the shadow of the newly unveiled bronze. Sojourner Truth had finally arrived in Washington—and this time, she is here to stay.

"Now, many of us—including myself—are here today because of the journey that Sojourner Truth began so long ago," Obama said. "We are here today because we stand on the shoulders of giants like Sojourner Truth."

Born Isabella Bomfree into slavery in New York in 1797, Truth escaped to freedom in 1826 and went on to become one of the nation's most formidable advocates for the abolition of slavery and universal suffrage.

After becoming a devout Christian, she changed her name to Sojourner Truth in 1843 and dedicated her life to traveling the country to speak out against slavery and in favor of women’s suffrage. The bust now stands prominently in Emancipation Hall, where millions of visitors to the Capitol will pass by each year. As Michelle Obama noted in her closing remarks, the monument ensures that Truth’s story will continue to inspire generations to come.
